evidence: Full ma explicitly explains the replacement of old aham by the oblique/instrumental pronoun (Prakrit maē, Apabhramsha maï̃), listing Assamese maï, Bengali mui, Oriya mu/mũ and Punjabi/Lahnda maĩ/mɛ̃. These whole first-person singular responses match those regional nominative continuations, preserving length, nasalization and source vowel notation. They are not assigned to aham merely from their nominative function; accusative molā and additional case endings are excluded.

The full tuvam article separates nominative, accusative, instrumental, genitive and dative developments; its addendum explicitly supplies Assamese tui. Hajong toi/tui is the neighboring familiar singular nominative and matches this complete regional pronoun. The link retains Turner’s discussion of analogical reshaping within the nominative family and leaves regional transmission open.

Full nava explicitly lists Khowar noγ “new, first day of lunar month”. These Khowar nox survey adjectives match that specific velar-final continuation, with the recorded voiceless fricative retained, rather than being assigned to the separate navala or naviya families.

Full nava lists Oriya nūā/lūā and western Gujarati navũ, Marathi navā and Hindi nawā, with Prakrit ṇa(v)a. These vowel/glide and v/b forms retain the corresponding plain new-adjective stem; source dot and nasalization notation are preserved. This is a regional family link, leaving contact open; forms with a lexical l/n extension and ambiguous short nai are excluded.

Section 2 naviya explicitly gives Prakrit ṇavia and Hindi/Bihari nayā, with feminine naī. These Tharu survey nayā/nayā̃ forms preserve the full y-bearing masculine adjective and fit that branch. The comparative-family relation does not settle whether Hindi transmission helped spread this form locally; bare nai forms ambiguous with nava feminine are excluded.

The first chagala branch explicitly supplies Torwali čhāl, Bashkarik čhēl and Maiya ċael, alongside Prakrit chēla. The selected local vowel and aspiration variants match those named goat comparanda; both alternatives in the selected Maiya response belong to the same family. This exact regional evidence is stronger than a generic chāgala similarity, and other languages are not automatically included.

Section 1 chagala includes Oriya cheḷi and Bihari/Hindi cherī “goat”, in the same chēla family. These eastern survey ceṛi/ceḍī responses match that feminine goat series with loss or variation of aspiration and the source’s retroflex/flap notation retained. The link leaves contact across neighboring eastern languages open.

Turner separates section 4 *chaggala, with Bihari chāgar/chāgrī and Awadhi chagarī “goat”, from the contracted chēl branch. These selected Danuwar, Majhi and Tharu c(h)agar/cegar forms retain medial g and r and match that specific regional branch. Extra -iyā material is excluded; local borrowing remains unresolved by the comparative link.
